01 · Overview

Ordering shouldn’t need a helper

01

The product

DinO is the NukkadShops restaurant ecosystem: an admin portal to set things up, a central dashboard for menus, POS and kitchen display systems for staff, and a self-order kiosk for customers.

02

The challenge

Kiosks in malls and food courts serve strangers in a hurry. They must work for one restaurant or many, in any order-type setup, with nobody around to explain.

03

The brief

Design a self-order kiosk that lets a first-time customer order confidently, in any restaurant setup the admin configures, from first tap to order number.

02 · The ecosystem

Five products, one order

The kiosk is only the customer-facing end of a pipeline. What it shows, who it sells for and where an order goes are all decided upstream.

Simplified for clarity. Numbers match the table below.

ProductUsed byWhat it doesTalks to the kiosk by
1 · Admin PortalPlatform adminCreates restaurants and groups, maps restaurants to a group, sets the group’s menu type (Common or Individual), enables Dine-in / Takeaway, creates kiosks, maps one or many restaurants to each kiosk and sets kiosk branding.Kiosk mappingBrandingOrder types
2 · Central DashboardGroup manager (group login)Sees all restaurants of the group, downloads the menu spreadsheet, edits items, prices and descriptions, uploads it back and submits it for approval. Nothing reaches a kiosk until it is approved.Approved menusPrices
3 · Kiosk deviceCustomers (staff log in once)Shows only the restaurants mapped to that kiosk, lets people browse, add, review, pay and collect an order number. Group credentials are never asked of a customer.OrdersPayment result
4 · POSRestaurant counter staffReceives the order and payment, handles billing, offers and sales reports for the restaurant.Order + payment in
5 · KDSKitchen staffShows live tickets per restaurant, tracks preparation and marks orders ready.Ticket inReady status out

Working personas drawn from product knowledge of food-court ordering. They are the lens used for decisions and are due to be validated in testing.

🥡

Ananya, 24

Lunch-break regular

Wants: to order in under two minutes and get back to work.

Struggles with: small text, not seeing what a dish looks like, not knowing if she can mix restaurants.

👨‍👩‍👧

Orders for the family

Struggles with: being forced to pick a restaurant before he knows what he wants.

🧑‍🍳

Kavya

Counter staff

Wants: fewer “can you help me?” moments and clean tickets per restaurant.

Struggles with: orders with no name or number, and orders that span more than one restaurant.

Order type not offered → switch prompt · details required

↺ Kitchen and counter receive the order at step 10; the order number is what the customer carries to pick-up.
06 · Key decisions

Four design decisions

Flow

Pick a restaurant or just pick a dish

Challenge: at a food court people rarely know the restaurant before they know the dish.

Decision: Home shows categories, popular picks and restaurants together. Food-first picks let people add straight away.

Both paths lead to the same cart.
Order logic

One order from one restaurant

Challenge: a food-court kiosk serves several kitchens, but POS and KDS tickets are per restaurant.

Decision: each order holds dishes from a single restaurant. Adding from another restaurant asks to start a new order, and nothing is cleared silently.

Clean tickets for every kitchen.
Imagery

Every dish gets its own picture

Challenge: dozens of similar dishes, like 30 beers, have to be told apart at a glance.

Decision: branded product photos where available, and generated pack illustrations (type, quantity, brand colour, size) for the rest.

Photo or art, no dish looks like another.
Checkout

Name and number before payment

Challenge: every order needs a way to reach the customer when it’s ready.

Decision: both are required. The button looks muted with a hint, and errors appear next to the field, not in a pop-up.

Every order is traceable.

09 · Measuring success

How we’ll know it works

The redesign is built and demo-ready. These are the measures to track once kiosks are live, so the case study can close with real numbers.

Speed

Time to first item

From Tap to Start to the first ADD.

Target to set after pilot
Completion

Order abandonment

Carts started vs. orders paid, split by step.

Compare against current kiosk
Independence

Assisted orders

How often staff step in to help a customer.

Log at the counter for two weeks
Discovery

Popular-pick conversion

Share of orders that begin from the picks row.

Event tracking on ADD source
Reliability

Payment failures

Failed vs. retried vs. abandoned payments.

Per method: UPI, gateway, card
Clarity

Usability test

Task: order a meal from two restaurants without help.

8 participants, think-aloud

Design for the worst screen

System bars, glare and arm’s-length reading decide legibility more than any style choice.

Respect the pipeline

Approval states, mapping and order types come from upstream. The kiosk has to look right in every combination.

Make the safe path the easy one

Confirming before clearing a cart and requiring contact details cost a tap and prevent a support call.
